notes: \cpara{Opens by recalling two earlier warnings: against envying ``crazy groups'' (``Why Our Kind Can't Cooperate'') and against copying religion (``Is Humanism A Religion-Substitute?''). The quoted line on atheistic hymns matches the earlier post.}

\cpara{States the premise: religion fills some needs worth filling. ``Is Humanism A Religion-Substitute?'' had rejected the assumption that everyone who is not religious ``has a hole in their mind that wants filling,'' while granting that some atheists have ``religion-shaped holes.'' This post names one such need, community, and does not say that every nonbeliever has it.}

\cpara{The post's main premise: the largest gap would be community. The first sentence is unhedged; the guess about half-believers that follows is hedged (``I would guess\ldots\ probably quite a lot''), and the next paragraph adds ``this is probably something I don't understand all that well.''}

\cfact{Later research supports the premise in general form. Lim and Putnam (\textsc{American Sociological Review}, 2010), using panel data, report that religious people are more satisfied with their lives ``because they regularly attend religious services and build social networks in their congregations,'' and find ``little evidence'' that private aspects of religiosity matter apart from attendance and congregational friendship. The study does not test the post's specific guess about people who stay without believing.}
\cpara{Admits uncertainty about what churches actually provide, and moves the question to what a hunter-gatherer band gives its people and what modern life lacks.}
\cpara{Sets the task: fill the emotional gap without copying the forms of church.}
\cpara{Offers workplaces as a second, accidental source of community, available only to the lucky.}
\cpara{The observation the proposals rest on: neither a church nor a workplace was designed to serve as a community.}
\cpara{Introduces the list as suspicions that ``would be better tested experimentally,'' and the last item repeats the call for data.}

\cfact{The link is to a 2005 Marginal Revolution post by Tyler Cowen, ``Why don't people have more sex?'' The claim about churches' ``medieval moralities'' is hedged with ``probably'' and comes without evidence.}

\cpara{Defines ``optimal'' as optimal for a community built as a community, and grants that spending on religion makes sense for people who want religion. The definition keeps the list from being a verdict on churches as churches.}
\cpara{A personal impression, offered as a confession, and a sketch of a building designed from scratch: time-shared between communities, with a large screen for talks and teaching.}

\cfact{For information, church buildings are already widely shared. Partners for Sacred Places, a nonprofit that supports historic religious buildings, reports that in its 1998 study ``81\% of those served by programs housed by congregations came from outside the congregation,'' and that in a later study of 90 congregations ``only 9\% of those four-million-odd visits were for worship'' (Jaeger and Stackhouse, Canopy Forum, 2023). The figures are the organization's own.}

\cpara{Weighs a rainy-day fund or insurance in place of mutual help, and partly rejects it (``Possibly not''). Then says churches provide community without admitting that this is ``nearly all of what people get out of it.''}

\cfact{Regular churchgoers describe their reasons differently. In a Pew Research Center survey (2018), eight in ten Americans who attend at least monthly called becoming ``closer to God'' a very important reason, and ``about one-in-twenty'' named being part of ``a community of faith'' as the main reason. Stated reasons need not measure what people get from attending, and the Lim and Putnam finding noted above points the other way. ``Nearly all'' goes beyond both.}
\cpara{Gives one example of what explicit design would change: welcoming newcomers right after a move, when they most need a community. The ``quarterly exhibitions'' are a joke.}
\cpara{Raises the objection that a community may need a purpose beyond itself.}
\cpara{Begins to answer yes, then corrects itself: bands had a purpose, survival. The correction leads into the next paragraph.}
\cpara{Turns from community for its own sake to communities formed around a shared goal.}

\cfact{The study cited above bears on this turn. Lim and Putnam found that the benefit of friends in a congregation was ``contingent, however, on the presence of a strong religious identity.'' Whether a shared secular goal can play that part, as the post proposes, the study does not test.}

\cpara{States the obstacle named in ``Can Humanism Match Religion's Output?'' the day before: rationalists are ``geographically distributed way the hell all over the place.'' That post promised ``some long-term, starry-eyed, idealistic thoughts on this particular problem''; this post supplies them. The judgment on the Internet is hedged (``does not seem'') and dated (``at the current stage of the technology'').}

\cpara{The proposal: rationalist communities as local taskforces working on the world's problems, each formed around the most specific shared interest that can support ``a decent-sized band.'' It is offered as what the author ``would like to see.'' The numbers fit the author's ``Dunbar's Function'' (2008), which gives ``30-50'' as ``a typical size for a cohesive hunter-gatherer band.''}
\cpara{Gives the reasons: such tasks need communities anyway, and the energy spent on religious institutions could go to them instead.}
\cpara{Restates the proposal in one line, for ``whatever fraction of humanity'' gets that far.}
\cpara{Adds adult learning as another possible center, since colleges ``seem to support communities quite well.''}

\cpara{Rates the proposal ``Maybe. Probably.'' a dream, with some ``incremental implementability,'' and closes on the direction the author would like: ``new idioms of community,'' not ``artificial churches.''}
